newsitem.title: GERMANY: German magazine says U.S. spy wanted Iran info.
newsitem.headline: German magazine says U.S. spy wanted Iran info.

text.p: The German news magazine Der Spiegel said on Sunday said a U.S. diplomat ordered out of the country for spying was digging for information about Germany's controversial trade ties with Iran.
The alleged spy and his predecessor, who left Bonn last year, tried to get a senior Economics Ministry official to name German firms selling high-tech equipment to Iran, it said.

They also asked about Bonn's official credit guarantees for German exports to Iran, a German-built nuclear plant in Iran, the 1995 expulsion of two Iranian spies from Bonn and a Berlin murder trial at which German prosecutors have accused Tehran of state terrorism, it said.

Spiegel said the German official, who is responsible for the Middle East and Iran at the Economics Ministry, reported the contacts to Germany's counter- intelligence agency, the Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV).
Officials at the BfV, the U.S. embassy and the Economics Ministry were not available for comment on the report.
Spiegel first reported the unprecedented expulsion last week, but gave no names or details of the connection with Iran. U.S. officials declined to comment on the charge.
Spiegel said the first contacts were made in 1994, when a U.S. diplomat began inviting the German official to dinner every three or four weeks to question him about his work, particularly with Iran.

The official refused to give detailed information, but the American kept trying and plied him with gifts. When the American left Germany in May last year, he introduced his successor to the German official.
The BfV pounced after the second U.S. spy quizzed the German official about the planned expansion of the German-built nuclear power following the official's visit to Tehran.
BfV boss Peter Frisch told the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) station chief in Bonn that the spy should leave Germany.
The station chief disputed the charges and asked for complete discretion in the case, but promised the spy would leave the country by the end of May, Spiegel said.
Spiegel said the case recalled France's expulsion in 1995 of four CIA operatives posing as diplomats for trying to buy information on the country's stance in global trade talks.
"Six and a half years after reunification and the end of the special rights of Allied forces... and Germany is still not master of its own house," wrote Spiegel.

U.S. sources told the Washington Post last week the agent was expelled to emphasise a new demand by Germany that it be kept informed of CIA operations inside its borders, not because of anger that it was gathering economic intelligence.
Germany, Iran's largest trade partner, maintains a policy of "critical dialogue" with the country as an alternative to the U.S. strategy of isolation.
